Main.sentence: An election is a formal ___E:group decision-making U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_decision-making)___ process whereby a ___E:population U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population)___ chooses an individual or multiple individuals to hold ___E:public office U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_administration)___ .
Elections have been the usual mechanism by which modern ___E:representative democracy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representative_democracy)___ has operated since the 17th century.

Elections may fill offices in the ___E:legislature U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislature)___ , sometimes in the ___E:executive U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_(government))___ and ___E:judiciary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judiciary)___ , and for ___E:regional and local government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_government)___ .

This process is also used in many other Standardized Associations, ___E:public businesses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business)___ , and organizations , from clubs to ___E:voluntary association U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voluntary_association)___ and ___E:corporations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporation)___ .

The global use of elections as a tool for selecting representatives in modern representative democracies is in contrast with the practice in the democratic ___E:archetype U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archetype)___ , ancient ___E:Athens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Athens)___ , where the elections were considered an ___E:oligarchic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oligarchy)___ institution and most political offices were filled using allotment which is also known as "Sortition", by which office holders were chosen by lot.

___E:Electoral reform U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_reform)___ describes the process of introducing fair ___E:electoral systems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_system)___ where they are not in place, or improving the fairness or effectiveness of existing systems. ___E:Psephology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psephology)___ is the study of results and other ___E:statistics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics)___ relating to elections (especially with a view to predicting future results).
Election is the fact of electing, or being elected.

To elect means "to select or to Nominate", and so sometimes other forms of ballot such as ___E:referendums U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referendum)___ are referred to as elections, especially in the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ .

Elections were used as early in history as ___E:ancient Greece U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece)___ and ___E:ancient Rome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome)___ , and throughout the ___E:Medieval period U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages)___ to select rulers such as the ___E:Holy Roman Emperor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Emperor)___ (see ___E:imperial election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_election)___ ) and the ___E:pope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope)___ (see ___E:papal election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_election)___ ).

The ___E:Pala U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pala_Empire)___ King ___E:Gopala U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gopala_(Pala_king))___ (ruled c. 750s – 770s CE) in early medieval ___E:Bengal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal)___ was elected by a group of feudal chieftains.
Such elections were quite common in contemporary societies of the region.

In the ___E:Chola Empire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chola_Empire)___ , around 920 CE, in ___E:Uthiramerur U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uthiramerur)___ (in present-day ___E:Tamil Nadu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamil_Nadu)___ ), palm leaves were used for selecting the village committee members.
The leaves, with candidate names written on them, were put inside a mud pot. To select the committee members, a young boy was asked to take out as many leaves as the number of positions available.
This was known as the Kudavolai system.

The first recorded popular elections of officials to public office, by majority vote, where all citizens were eligible both to vote and to hold public office, date back to the ___E:Ephors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephors)___ of ___E:Sparta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparta)___ in 754 BC, under the ___E:mixed government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_government)___ of the ___E:Spartan Constitution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spartan_Constitution)___ .   ___E:Athenian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenian)___ democratic elections, where all citizens could hold public office, were not introduced for another 247 years, until the reforms of ___E:Cleisthenes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleisthenes)___ .

Under the earlier ___E:Solonian Constitution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solonian_Constitution)___ ( c. 574 BC ), all Athenian citizens were eligible to vote in the popular assemblies, on matters of law and policy, and as jurors, but only the three highest classes of citizens could vote in elections.

Nor were the lowest of the four classes of Athenian citizens (as defined by the extent of their wealth and property, rather than by birth) eligible to hold public office, through the reforms of ___E:Solon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solon)___ .
The Spartan election of the Ephors, therefore, also predates the reforms of Solon in Athens by approximately 180 years.
Questions of ___E:suffrage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffrage)___ , especially suffrage for minority groups, have dominated the history of elections.
Males, the dominant cultural group in North America and Europe, often dominated the ___E:electorate U:(https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/electorate)___ and continue to do so in many countries.

Early elections in countries such as the ___E:United Kingdom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_the_United_Kingdom)___ and ___E:the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_the_United_States)___ were dominated by ___E:landed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landed_gentry)___ or ___E:ruling class U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruling_class)___ males.

By 1920 all Western European and North American democracies had universal adult male suffrage (except Switzerland) and many countries began to consider ___E:women's suffrage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women%27s_suffrage)___ .

Despite legally mandated universal suffrage for adult males, political barriers were sometimes erected to prevent fair access to elections (see ___E:civil rights movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement)___ ).
Elections are held in a variety of political, organizational, and corporate settings.

Many countries hold elections to select people to serve in their governments, but other types of organizations hold elections as well. For example, many corporations hold elections among ___E:shareholders U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shareholders)___ to select a ___E:board of directors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_directors)___ , and these elections may be mandated by ___E:corporate law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_law)___ .

In many places, an election to the government is usually a competition among people who have already won a ___E:primary election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partisan_primary)___ within a ___E:political party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_party)___ .
Elections within corporations and other organizations often use procedures and rules that are similar to those of governmental elections.
The question of who may vote is a central issue in elections.
The electorate does not generally include the entire population; for example, many countries prohibit those who are under the age of majority from voting.
All jurisdictions require a minimum age for voting.

In Australia, ___E:Aboriginal people U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aboriginal_people)___ were not given the right to vote until 1962 (see ___E:1967 referendum entry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_referendum,_1967_(Aboriginals))___ ) and in 2010 the federal government removed the rights of prisoners serving for three years or more to vote (a large proportion of whom were Aboriginal Australians).
Suffrage is typically only for citizens of the country, though further limits may be imposed.
In the European Union, one can vote in municipal elections if one lives in the municipality and is an EU citizen; the nationality of the country of residence is not required.

In some countries, voting is required by law. Eligible voters may be subject to punitive measures such as a fine for not casting a vote. In Western Australia, the penalty for a first time offender failing to vote is a $20.00 fine, which increases to $50.00 if the offender refused to vote prior.

Historically the size of eligible voters, the electorate, was small having the size of groups or communities of privileged men like ___E:aristocrats U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristocrats)___ and men of a city ( ___E:citizens U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizens#History)___ ).

With the growth of the number of people with ___E:bourgeois U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourgeoisie)___ citizen rights outside of cities, expanding the term citizen, the electorates grew to numbers beyond the thousands.

Elections with an electorate in the hundred thousands appeared in the final decades of the ___E:Roman Republic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_the_Roman_Republic)___ , by extending voting rights to citizens outside of Rome with the ___E:Lex Julia of 90 BC U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Julia#Lex_Iulia_de_Civitate_Latinis_et_Sociis_Danda_(90_BC))___ , reaching an electorate of 910,000 and estimated ___E:voter turnout U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voter_turnout)___ of maximum 10% in 70 BC,  only again comparable in size to the ___E:first elections of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1788%E2%80%9389_United_States_elections)___ .

At the same time the ___E:Kingdom of Great Britain U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Great_Britain)___ had in 1780 about 214,000 eligible voters, 3% of the whole population.  ___E:Naturalization U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalization)___ can reshape the electorate of a country.
A ___E:representative democracy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representative_democracy)___ requires a procedure to govern nomination for political office.
In many cases, nomination for office is mediated through ___E:preselection U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preselection)___ processes in organized political parties.
Non-partisan systems tend to be different from partisan systems as concerns nominations.

In a ___E:direct democracy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_democracy)___ , one type of ___E:non-partisan democracy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-partisan_democracy)___ , any eligible person can be nominated.

Although elections were used in ancient Athens, in Rome, and in the selection of popes and Holy Roman emperors, the origins of elections in the contemporary world lie in the gradual emergence of representative government in Europe and North America beginning in the 17th century.

In some systems no nominations take place at all, with voters free to choose any person at the time of voting—with some possible exceptions such as through a minimum age requirement—in the jurisdiction.

In such cases, it is not required (or even possible) that the members of the electorate be familiar with all of the eligible persons, though such systems may involve ___E:indirect elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indirect_election)___ at larger geographic levels to ensure that some first-hand familiarity among potential electees can exist at these levels (i.e., among the elected delegates).
Electoral systems are the detailed constitutional arrangements and voting systems that convert the vote into a political decision.

The first step is for voters to cast the ___E:ballots U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballot)___ , which may be simple single-choice ballots, but other types, such as multiple choice or ___E:ranked ballots U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranked_voting)___ may also be used. Then the votes are tallied, for which various ___E:vote counting systems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vote_counting_systems)___ may be used. and the voting system then determines the result on the basis of the tally.

Most systems can be categorized as either ___E:proportional U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_representation)___ , ___E:majoritarian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majoritarian)___ or ___E:mixed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_electoral_system)___ .

Among the proportional systems, the most commonly used are ___E:party-list proportional representation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party-list_proportional_representation)___ (list PR) systems, among majoritarian are ___E:first-past-the-post U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-past-the-post_voting)___ electoral system (single winner ___E:plurality voting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurality_voting)___ ) and different methods of majority voting (such as the widely used ___E:two-round system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-round_system)___ ). ___E:Mixed systems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_electoral_system)___ combine elements of both proportional and majoritarian methods, with some typically producing results closer to the former ( ___E:mixed-member proportional U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-member_proportional_representation)___ ) or the other (e.g. ___E:parallel voting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_voting)___ ).

Many countries have growing electoral reform movements, which advocate systems such as ___E:approval voting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Approval_voting)___ , ___E:single transferable vote U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_transferable_vote)___ , ___E:instant runoff voting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instant-runoff_voting)___ or a ___E:Condorcet method U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condorcet_method)___ ; these methods are also gaining popularity for lesser elections in some countries where more important elections still use more traditional counting methods.

While openness and ___E:accountability U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accountability)___ are usually considered cornerstones of a democratic system, the act of casting a vote and the content of a voter's ballot are usually an important exception.

The ___E:secret ballot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret_ballot)___ is a relatively modern development, but it is now considered crucial in most ___E:free and fair elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_and_fair_election)___ , as it limits the effectiveness of intimidation.
When elections are called, politicians and their supporters attempt to influence policy by competing directly for the votes of constituents in what are called campaigns.
Supporters for a campaign can be either formally organized or loosely affiliated, and frequently utilize ___E:campaign advertising U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaign_advertising)___ .
It is common for political scientists to attempt to predict elections via ___E:political forecasting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_forecasting)___ methods.

The most expensive election campaign included US$7 billion spent on the ___E:2012 United States presidential election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_presidential_election)___ and is followed by the US$5 billion spent on the ___E:2014 Indian general election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Indian_general_election)___ .

The nature of democracy is that elected officials are accountable to the people, and they must return to the voters at prescribed intervals to seek their ___E:mandate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandate_(politics))___ to continue in office.
For that reason, most democratic constitutions provide that elections are held at fixed regular intervals.

In the United States, elections for public offices are typically held between every two and six years in most states and at the federal level, with exceptions for elected judicial positions that may have longer terms of office.

There is a variety of schedules, for example, presidents: the ___E:President of Ireland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Ireland)___ is elected every seven years, the ___E:President of Russia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Russia)___ and the ___E:President of Finland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Finland)___ every six years, the ___E:President of France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France)___ every five years, ___E:President of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States)___ every four years.
Predetermined or fixed election dates have the advantage of fairness and predictability.

They tend to greatly lengthen campaigns, [citation needed] and make ___E:dissolving the legislature U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_parliament)___ (parliamentary system) more problematic if the date should happen to fall at a time when dissolution is inconvenient (e.g. when war breaks out).

Other states (e.g., the ___E:United Kingdom U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom)___ ) only set maximum time in office, and the executive decides exactly when within that limit it will actually go to the polls.

In practice, this means the government remains in power for close to its full term, and chooses an election date it calculates to be in its best interests (unless something special happens, such as a ___E:motion of no-confidence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_of_no-confidence)___ ).
This calculation depends on a number of variables, such as its performance in opinion polls and the size of its majority.
Postponing elections beyond the full term has been associated with ___E:democratic backsliding U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_backsliding)___ .

Rolling elections are elections in which all ___E:representatives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representative_democracy)___ in a body are elected, but these elections are spread over a period of time rather than all at once. Examples are the presidential ___E:primaries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primaries)___ in the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ , ___E:Elections to the European Parliament U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_to_the_European_Parliament)___ (where, due to differing election laws in each member state, elections are held on different days of the same week) and, due to logistics, general elections in ___E:Lebanon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Lebanon)___ and ___E:India U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_India)___ .
The voting procedure in the ___E:Legislative Assemblies of the Roman Republic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_Assemblies_of_the_Roman_Republic)___ are also a classical example.
In rolling elections, voters have information about previous voters' choices.
While in the first elections, there may be plenty of hopeful candidates, in the last rounds consensus on one winner is generally achieved.
In today's context of rapid communication, candidates can put disproportionate resources into competing strongly in the first few stages, because those stages affect the reaction of latter stages.

In many of the countries with weak ___E:rule of law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_law)___ , the most common reason why elections do not meet international standards of being "free and fair" is interference from the incumbent government. ___E:Dictators U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictator)___ may use the powers of the executive (police, martial law, censorship, physical implementation of the election mechanism, etc.) to remain in power despite popular opinion in favour of removal.

Members of a particular faction in a legislature may use the power of the majority or supermajority (passing criminal laws, and defining the electoral mechanisms including eligibility and district boundaries) to prevent the balance of power in the body from shifting to a rival faction due to an election.
Non-governmental entities can also interfere with elections, through physical force, verbal intimidation, or fraud, which can result in improper casting or counting of votes.
Monitoring for and minimizing electoral fraud is also an ongoing task in countries with strong traditions of free and fair elections.
Problems that prevent an election from being "free and fair" take various forms.

The electorate may be poorly informed about issues or candidates due to lack of ___E:freedom of the press U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press)___ , lack of objectivity in the press due to state or corporate control, or lack of access to news and political media. ___E:Freedom of speech U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_speech)___ may be curtailed by the state, favouring certain viewpoints or state ___E:propaganda U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propaganda)___ .
Scheduling ___E:frequent elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frequent_elections)___ can also lead to ___E:voter fatigue U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voter_fatigue)___ .

___E:Gerrymandering U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerrymandering)___ , ___E:wasted votes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasted_vote)___ and manipulating ___E:electoral thresholds U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_threshold)___ can prevent that all votes count equally.

Exclusion of opposition candidates from eligibility for office, needlessly high ___E:nomination rules U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomination_rules)___ on who may be a candidate, are some of the ways the structure of an election can be changed to favour a specific faction or candidate.

Those in power may arrest or assassinate candidates, suppress or even criminalize campaigning, close campaign headquarters, harass or beat campaign workers, or intimidate voters with violence. ___E:Foreign electoral intervention U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_electoral_intervention)___ can also occur, with the United States interfering between 1946 and 2000 in 81 elections and ___E:Russia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia)___ or the ___E:Soviet Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union)___ in 36.  In 2018 the most intense interventions, utilizing false information, were by ___E:China U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China)___ in ___E:Taiwan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan)___ and by ___E:Russia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia)___ in ___E:Latvia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latvia)___ ; the next highest levels were in Bahrain, Qatar and Hungary.

This can include falsifying voter instructions,  violation of the ___E:secret ballot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secret_ballot)___ , ___E:ballot stuffing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballot_stuffing)___ , tampering with voting machines,  destruction of legitimately cast ballots,  ___E:voter suppression U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voter_suppression)___ , voter registration fraud, failure to validate voter residency, fraudulent tabulation of results, and use of physical force or verbal intimation at polling places.
Other examples include persuading candidates not to run, such as through blackmailing, bribery, intimidation or physical violence.
A sham election , or show election is an election that is held purely for show; that is, without any significant political choice or real impact on the results of the election.

Sham elections are a common event in ___E:dictatorial regimes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictatorship)___ that feel the need to feign the appearance of public ___E:legitimacy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legitimacy_(political))___ .

Published results usually show high ___E:voter turnout U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voter_turnout)___ and high support (typically at least 80%, and close to 100% in many cases) for the prescribed candidates or for the ___E:referendum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referendum)___ choice that favours the ___E:political party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_party)___ in power.
Dictatorial regimes can also organize sham elections with results simulating those that might be achieved in democratic countries.

Sometimes, only one government-approved candidate is allowed to run in sham elections with no opposition candidates allowed, or opposition candidates are arrested on false charges (or even without any charges) before the election to prevent them from running.

Ballots may contain only one "yes" option, or in the case of a simple "yes or no" question, security forces often ___E:persecute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution)___ people who pick "no", thus encouraging them to pick the "yes" option.

In other cases, those who vote receive stamps in their passport for doing so, while those who did not vote (and thus do not receive stamps) are persecuted as ___E:enemies of the people U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enemy_of_the_people)___ .
Sham elections can sometimes backfire against the party in power, especially if the regime believes they are popular enough to win without coercion, fraud or suppressing the opposition.

The most famous example of this was the ___E:1990 Myanmar general election U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Myanmar_general_election)___ , in which the government-sponsored ___E:National Unity Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Unity_Party_(Myanmar))___ suffered a landslide defeat by the opposition ___E:National League for Democracy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_League_for_Democracy)___ and consequently, the results were annulled.

Some scholars argue that the predominance of elections in modern ___E:liberal democracies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_democracy)___ masks the fact that they are actually aristocratic selection mechanisms  that deny each citizen an equal chance of holding public office.
Such views were expressed as early as the time of ___E:Ancient Greece U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece)___ by ___E:Aristotle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle)___ .

According to French ___E:political scientist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science)___ Bernard Manin, the inegalitarian nature of elections stems from four factors: the unequal treatment of candidates by voters, the distinction of candidates required by choice, the cognitive advantage conferred by salience, and the costs of disseminating information.
These four factors result in the evaluation of candidates based on voters' partial standards of quality and social saliency (for example, skin colour and good looks).
This leads to self-selection biases in candidate pools due to unobjective standards of treatment by voters and the costs (barriers to entry) associated with raising one's political profile.

Ultimately, the result is the election of candidates who are superior (whether in actuality or as perceived within a cultural context) and objectively unlike the voters they are supposed to represent.
Evidence suggests that the concept of electing representatives was originally conceived to be different from ___E:democracy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy)___ .

Prior to the 18th century, some societies in ___E:Western Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe)___ used ___E:sortition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sortition)___ as a means to select rulers, a method which allowed regular citizens to exercise power, in keeping with understandings of democracy at the time.  The idea of what constituted a legitimate government shifted in the 18th century to include ___E:consent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consent_of_the_governed)___ , especially with the rise of the ___E:enlightenment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment)___ .
From this point onward, sortition fell out of favor as a mechanism for selecting rulers.
On the other hand, elections began to be seen as a way for the masses to express popular consent repeatedly, resulting in the triumph of the electoral process until the present day.

This conceptual misunderstanding of elections as open and egalitarian when they are not innately so may thus be a root cause of the ___E:problems in contemporary governance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oligarchy)___ .

Those in favor of this view argue that the modern system of elections was never meant to give ordinary citizens the chance to exercise power - merely privileging their right to consent to those who rule.  Therefore, the representatives that modern electoral systems select for are too disconnected, unresponsive, and elite-serving.
To deal with this issue, various scholars have proposed alternative models of democracy, many of which include a return to sortition-based selection mechanisms.
The extent to which sortition should be the dominant mode of selecting rulers  or instead be hybridised with electoral representation  remains a topic of debate.
